Seif katan 2, "They train," etc. See Tosafot. This appears in Tosafot Yeshanim and likewise in Terumat HaDeshen, siman 94. They ask about the Mishnah in Yoma 82, which states that minors are trained to fast for hours. Yet when a minor eats prohibited foods, beit din is not commanded to separate him. If they are not commanded even to separate him, how can there be a command to train him? Rabbeinu Yitzchak answers that the mitzvah of chinuch rests specifically upon the father, not upon another person. Therefore others are not commanded to separate the child.

Tosafot then ask from the beginning of Sukkah, where Queen Helena sat in a sukkah with her 7 sons. This indicates that chinuch applies even where the father is absent. They answer that perhaps the children had a father who trained them in this mitzvah; and even if they did not, their mother trained them merely as a voluntary mitzvah practice. The same appears in Terumat HaDeshen. Tosafot write similarly in Nazir 28b, while on 29a the Gemara expressly concludes according to Reish Lakish that a mother is not obligated to train her son. Although R' Yochanan disputes Reish Lakish there and does not require that conclusion for his own explanation, it is preferable to minimize the dispute and say that R' Yochanan agrees on this point. See Magen Avraham, siman 343.

"Nevertheless, it appears to me that she should not give," etc. Meaning the mother, although she is not obligated in chinuch.

"And it is not comparable to sukkah, where she is permitted," etc. Otherwise, what did Tosafot ask from Queen Helena sitting in a sukkah with her 7 sons? It would have been forbidden for her to give them food outside the sukkah.

"And she is not obligated to bring him in," etc., because the mother is not obligated in chinuch.

"Furthermore, there it is a positive commandment." Meaning that eating in a sukkah is a positive commandment. A negative prohibition is more severe than a positive commandment, as stated in the first chapter of Yevamos in the discussion of "aleha" and as also appears in the second chapter of Yevamos. This is the conclusion of Terumat HaDeshen, siman 94. Therefore, since eating in a sukkah involves only a positive commandment, even giving the child food is more lenient.

Magen Avraham at the beginning of siman 269, however, rejects this reasoning. We rule that one may not directly feed a minor even a rabbinically prohibited substance, all the more so one may not actively cause him to fail to fulfill a Torah positive commandment. We must therefore say that the principal answer remains the first one: sukkah is different because the act of eating itself is not prohibited. In truth, directly feeding a minor outside the sukkah is forbidden even for a woman, as Magen Avraham writes explicitly below in siman 640.

What he now adds is another distinction. Even if Yom Kippur were exactly analogous to sukkah regarding direct feeding, there is still more room for leniency in sukkah because it concerns a positive commandment, whereas eating on Yom Kippur is a negative prohibition. Terumat HaDeshen, however, concludes by challenging the cited Tosafot and proving from Eruvin that a mother too is obligated in her son's chinuch, and he therefore concludes that one should not be lenient.

"That which does not," etc., "in his 12th year." Meaning when he is 11 complete years old, as Rama writes that leniency should be used only for a weak youth.

"Because everyone studies," etc. We rely upon Rashi's view in Kesubos 50a according to Bach's interpretation of Rashi. When the child is 12 complete years old and enters his 13th year, however, Rashi and Bach agree that he must complete the fast rabbinically, except where he is weak, in which case we rely upon the opinion brought by Rama.

Eliyah Rabbah cites Bach regarding Rama's statement that one may rely on the lenient view for a weak youth, and writes that our custom is to treat all children this way because they all study, and nowadays they are generally considered weak. In truth, Bach was lenient only when the child was 11, as stated above. It is possible that Eliyah Rabbah wrote the broader point from his own reasoning based upon Bach. His further statement, that nowadays children are generally considered ill, means that weakness has increased in later generations. Bach concludes that since we are not expert in determining when a situation becomes a danger to life, a doubtful danger is treated leniently.

1) [Seif 1] "Although it is a mitzvah to articulate its letters precisely, if he read without precise articulation he fulfilled his obligation." Nevertheless, one must take care to articulate them precisely. Rav Chama bar Chanina said that whoever reads Kriat Shema precisely in its letters has Gehinnom cooled for him. Tur. Bach explains that one is halachically obligated to be careful about this. If he is careless, he is punished with the heat of Gehinnom; if he is careful, Gehinnom is cooled for him. A great matter therefore depends upon careful articulation of its letters.

I heard a mnemonic: from the letters of "Shema" and "Echad" remain the initials of Chananiah, Mishael, Azariah, and Daniel, alluding that one who recites Kriat Shema with proper intention is saved from fire as Chananiah, Mishael, Azariah, and Daniel were. Eliyah Rabbah, letter 1. See what we wrote above in siman 61, letters 1 and 56.

2) There, "If he read without precise articulation he fulfilled his obligation." Sefer HaChinuch, Parashat Vaetchanan, writes that this does not mean that he may omit words or letters, for one who did not read the entire Kriat Shema has not fulfilled his obligation. Rather, failure of precision means such matters as failing to leave sufficient space between adjacent sounds, failing to pronounce distinctly the zayin in tizkeru, or failing to extend the dalet of Echad for the proper amount of time, all of which should ideally be done. Eliyah Rabbah there; Pri Megadim, Eshel Avraham, letter 1.

Seif katan 3, "And they give," etc. Therefore it is sufficient when they give the wine to the infant receiving brit milah. It is forbidden to give it to other children lest they become accustomed to drinking on a fast day.

"Although when a brit milah occurs on Tisha B'Av, siman 559, seif 7, states that it is given to children." Since a brit milah does not occur on Tisha B'Av every year, we are not concerned that the children will become habituated. Yom Kippur, however, is Torah-level, and Rama therefore treated it more stringently than Tisha B'Av, as Magen Avraham writes above in siman 559.

"Levush wrote that since Minhagim states that they give it to children." Meaning to other children as well, not only to the infant receiving brit milah as Rama writes. Levush thus equates Yom Kippur with Tisha B'Av.

"Nevertheless, one must say, besides," etc. This refers to Rama's statement that it should be given to the infant receiving brit milah.

"And they give it to the infant receiving brit milah." The tasting of the cup is required only because it is unbecoming for people to say that this blessing was recited for no purpose. It is therefore sufficient to give some of it to such a small infant. [Raavan, chapter 3 of Eruvin] Responsa Ran, siman 52, however, writes in the name of Rashba that this remains a blessing in vain because the wine is given to such a young child. Levush writes that since Minhagim says simply that it is given to children, one should not protest against those who follow the lenient custom.

Nevertheless, it appears to me that besides placing some wine in the infant's mouth when saying "Through your blood, live," one should give him a little wine to drink from the cup itself. Otherwise there still remains a lack of dignity toward the cup. See Yoreh De'ah, siman 265, end of seif 1 and end of seif 4.

(14) "Which is not suitable for lying upon." The wording is not exact. If it were wholly unsuitable for lying upon, why would we say that by default it is intended for lying? Rather, it means that it is not especially suitable for lying, as Tur states explicitly.

(15) "If it is small." Meaning large enough for a person to lie upon.

(16) "By default it is intended for lying and can become tamei," etc. Since its ordinary purpose is lying upon, it is fit to become tamei when a zav lies upon it. Once it is fit to receive tumah, it is already disqualified for use as sechach, because anything fit to receive tumah may not be used for sechach.

(17) "Meaning that the majority," etc. If he made it explicitly for sechach, this is effective even in a place where there is no established local custom. Rama comes only to exclude the opposite case: if the local custom is to make such mats for lying upon, it does not help that this particular person made or purchased his mat explicitly for sechach, because other people do not know that and may come to use ordinary such mats for sechach. Sometimes local custom also creates leniency. If he made the mat without specifying its purpose, or we do not know whether he made it for sechach or lying upon, and most residents of the city make such mats for sechach, we assume that he too made it for sechach.

(18) "Unless he made it for lying, meaning," etc. This does not mean that if the local custom is for sechach, his own intention to use it for lying is ineffective. That is certainly false. Once he intended it for lying, the laws of tumah apply to it and it may not be used for sechach. The point is rather that not only an explicit act of making it for lying creates the problem; a local custom to use such mats for lying is likewise treated as though he himself made it for lying. If the local custom is unknown, everyone agrees that it may be used for sechach so long as we do not know that it was made for lying. In these countries all such mats are made for lying, so even if a person made one for sechach it should not be used.

(19) "In a manner that it is fit to hold." Since it is fit to serve as a receptacle, it has the status of a utensil and is capable of receiving tumah, and therefore may not be used for sechach. This applies where nothing was specified. In that case, a raised rim indicates that it was made to hold things and it consequently receives tumah. If, however, he expressly intended it for sechach, then according to some authorities it does not receive tumah even if it has a rim, because that receptacle-like form is insignificant when the object was not made for receiving. Other later authorities hold that once it has a rim it receives tumah in every case and may not be used for sechach.

(20) "Even if its rim was removed." It resembles other broken utensils, which the Sages prohibited for sechach, as explained above in seif 2.

(21) "They may not be used for sechach." Meaning even if they were made specifically for sechach and therefore do not receive tumah, the Sages decreed against using them lest a person sit under the roof of a house made from such mats. Mats fixed as part of a house roof are invalid by Torah law because they were installed for dwelling, not for shade.

5) [Seif 2] "One who wishes to be stringent," etc. Maharshal in Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma, chapter 7, siman 41, writes that a person who acts stringently in public regarding something permitted, where there is concern for religious ostentation, is subject to excommunication. If it is known that he acts for the sake of Heaven, he is not excommunicated. If he acts stringently in the presence of his Rav while his Rav rules leniently, however, he is subject to excommunication even if his intent is for the sake of Heaven. Even where the permission is not completely obvious, he should not act stringently against his Rav's ruling unless he has evidence that refutes it. Magen Avraham, seif katan 2; Soles Belulah, letter 2; Eliyah Rabbah, letter 4; Chesed LaAlafim, letter 2. See Pri Megadim, Eshel Avraham, and Machatzit HaShekel, letter 2.

Birkei Yosef, letter 1, cites Rabbi Menachem of Beit Meir, brought in Shitah Mekubetzet, Bava Kamma 81b, that where a matter's permissibility is obvious, it is improper to act stringently in the presence of one who is greater in wisdom while that scholar follows the lenient practice. If he does so, the greater scholar may excommunicate him. If the stringent person is known for piety, however, he may conduct himself stringently. See Responsa Maharadakh, end of responsum 26, and Ginnat Veradim, Yoreh De'ah, rule 3, end of siman 6.

6) There, "One who wishes to be stringent by standing when he had been sitting and reciting it standing is called a transgressor." Tur concludes in the name of Rav Amram that he should be rebuked, because its mitzvah is while seated. Beit Yosef explains that this means only that it may be recited even while seated. Perishah, letter 6, however, writes that it specifically should be recited seated. Rama in Darkei Moshe, letter 1, appears to agree. He cites Hagahot Maimoniyot, chapter 2, that sitting is preferable to standing, apparently disagreeing with Maran and holding that sitting is the preferred form.

Pri Chadash, letter 2, likewise explains Tur in the name of Rav Amram to mean that the principal mitzvah is seated, so that a person's mind is especially settled, similar to the conclusion at the end of Perek Sheloshah SheAchlu that in all those cases the halacha is that one sits and recites the blessing. Maamar Mordechai, letter 2, cites him and approves.

This is likewise implied by Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 48, on the verse, "He was sitting at the entrance of the tent." R' Berechyah in the name of R' Levi says that "sit" is written. Avraham wished to stand, but Hashem told him, "Sit." So too your descendants will sit: when Israel enters synagogues and study halls and recites Kriat Shema, they sit in My honor, while I stand over them, as it says, "God stands in the congregation of God." The same appears in Bamidbar Rabbah, Parashat Naso, chapter 11, and Midrash Chazita on "My Beloved resembles a gazelle." Yafeh LaLev, letter 2.

Shaar HaKavanos, discourse 2 concerning the repetition of the Amidah, and Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar Kriat Shema, end of chapter 29, likewise imply that since Kriat Shema corresponds to Beriah it should be recited seated. Although Shaar HaKavanos, discourse 6 concerning Kriat Shema, might imply that if one wished to say it standing this would not matter, according to the mystical teaching sitting remains preferable. See Ateret Zekenim, letter 2, and Ben Ish Chai, Parashat Vaera, letter 16.

7) There, "And recite it standing," etc. Sefer HaKanah, cited in the newer Tzafnat Paneach, states that in Eretz Yisrael Kriat Shema should be said standing and outside Eretz Yisrael seated. This distinction does not appear to be accepted by the halachic authorities or kabbalists. In Eretz Yisrael and outside it alike, "the righteous sit." Kaf HaChaim by Rabbi Chaim Palagi, siman 14, letter 32. This likewise follows from Shaar HaKavanos and Pri Etz Chaim cited in the preceding letter, because the reason for sitting is that Kriat Shema corresponds to Beriah, a reason that does not distinguish between Eretz Yisrael and outside it.

8) There, "He is called a transgressor." This implies that he nevertheless fulfilled his obligation. Even according to Rav Yosef, who says that one who acted like Beit Shammai "did nothing," the meaning is that he did not fulfill the mitzvah in its proper manner. The Gemara compares this with one whose head and most of his body were in a sukkah while his table remained inside the house, where after the fact he fulfilled the obligation. Ran writes similarly at the end of Arvei Pesachim regarding the Mishnah's statement that one who did not say these 3 things on Pesach did not fulfill his obligation. Ramban writes likewise in Milchamot at the beginning of Berachot, as does Tur at the end of siman 66. Erech HaShulchan, letter 1. See Mateh Yehudah, letter 1; Pithei HaDevir, letter 2; and Yafeh LaLev, letter 2.

9) There, "He is called a transgressor." If he stands merely in order to dispel sleep, it is permitted. Chesed LaAlafim, letter 2; Ben Ish Chai, Parashat Vaera, letter 15.

6) There, "One who wishes to be stringent by standing when he had been sitting and reciting it standing is called a transgressor." Tur concludes in the name of Rav Amram that he should be rebuked, because its mitzvah is while seated. Beit Yosef explains that this means only that it may be recited even while seated. Perishah, letter 6, however, writes that it specifically should be recited seated. Rama in Darkei Moshe, letter 1, appears to agree, since he cites Hagahot Maimoniyot, chapter 2, that it is preferable to recite it seated rather than standing.

Pri Chadash, letter 2, likewise explains Tur in the name of Rav Amram that the principal mitzvah is seated so that one's mind is especially settled, as we say at the end of Perek Sheloshah SheAchlu that in all those cases the halacha is to sit and recite the blessing. Maamar Mordechai, letter 2, cites him and writes that his words are correct.

The same appears from Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 48, on "He was sitting at the entrance of the tent." R' Berechyah in the name of R' Levi says that "sit" is written. Avraham wished to stand, but Hashem told him, "Sit." So too your descendants sit when Israel enters synagogues and study halls and recites Kriat Shema; they sit in My honor while I stand over them, as it is written, "God stands in the congregation of God." The same is found in Bamidbar Rabbah, Parashat Naso, chapter 11, and Midrash Chazita on "My Beloved resembles a gazelle." Yafeh LaLev, letter 2.

Shaar HaKavanos, discourse 2 concerning the repetition of the Amidah, and Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar Kriat Shema, end of chapter 29, likewise imply that because Kriat Shema corresponds to Beriah it should be recited seated. Although another passage in Shaar HaKavanos might imply that standing would not invalidate the recitation, according to the mystical structure sitting remains preferable. See Ateret Zekenim, letter 2, and Ben Ish Chai, Parashat Vaera, letter 16.
